utterances.text: Line 14: "If a person is just generally asked neutral, non-leading questions, isn't the research, that is not generally a problem?" Your answer: "No, that is not what the research says. If you ask any questions at all, it is a problem. If you ask neutral questions, it minimises the confabulation but it doesn't eradicate it. If you ask a leading question, it compounds it. But the issue of confabulation is built into the use of hypnosis or, better, to the hypnotisability and a certain characteristic of the particular patient." Is that your testimony in that case, Dr. Brown?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL BROWN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: So even questions like "Witness A, what happened to you?" assuming that she is highly hypnotisable, would confabulate her memory?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL BROWN
utterances.text: Your original question to me said "likely to confabulate" and that would mischaracterise things. We have a hierarchy here. Free recall minimises but doesn't eradicate distortion of memory. Asking specific questions causing a slight increase in the distortion rate, asking leading questions causes another rise, and asking systematic misleading questions causes a significant rise. So we're talking about on a continuum here. That continuum of supplying misinformation has to be weighed against the degree of memory suggestibility of that given individual. So let's say, for example, you have an extremely high memory suggestible individual. A small amount of misinformation can distort the memory. If you have somebody in the moderate or lower range, you'd have to systematically supply this information to get a significant distortion.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Doctor, let's look at page 276, please, line 13: "But when somebody brings up something upsetting, you are saying that Ms. Lauder is likely to be in some altered state?" Answer: "That's correct." Question: "And that's the basis for this --" Your answer: "Or if she brings up something upsetting, like the references to the fact that there was something about the previous therapy that bothered her, that's a situation in which she is more likely to go into trance." Question: "And that causes her to manufacture additional details about events --" Answer: "'Manufacture' is too intentional. I wouldn't say that." Question: "'Confabulate.' Excuse me. Is that the word?" Answer: "'Confabulate,' yes." Was that your testimony?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL BROWN
utterances.text: That's my testimony, but it's important to clarify here that the diagnosis of this patient, in addition to post-traumatic stress, was essentially multiple personality disorder now called dissociative identity disorder. People with multiple personality disorder score on the average 10.5; that puts them in the extreme high range of memory suggestibility. So the testimony here is very specific about a particular -- COURT REPORTER: I'm sorry, I'm getting the French interpretation on Channel 4.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: You have no idea what range of hypnotisability Witness A is in; correct?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL BROWN
utterances.text: No, I do not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And that really, absent independent corroboration, there is no way to determine whether she has been confabulating memories or whether she is accurate; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL BROWN
utterances.text: That's really for the triers of fact. It's not an expert question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: It is your opinion, Doctor, that in determining or evaluating a person, there is no way to determine whether they can -- whether they are telling you a true version of events or are confabulating memories if they are in the high hypnotisability range?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL BROWN
utterances.text: It would lower our confidence in the evidence, that's certainly true.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Right. But you would also say you need independent corroboration?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL BROWN
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Right. So in this particular case, can you determine whether Witness A was confabulating or not confabulating?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL BROWN
utterances.text: If you're asking me --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, that is the question that we are going to have to answer, isn't it? I don't think we are assisted by these generalised questions. That's my opinion.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: My point, Your Honour, is that he's taken a direct contrary position in a different case which was not revealed this morning with respect to the accuracy of sexual abuse victims in particular and trauma patients generally, and these factors about hypnotisability, et cetera, there is this significant element that a PTSD patient is in that very high hypnotisability range, and this is his testimony in this case.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: I must object to that, Your Honours. I am certain that at no time has Dr. Brown said in the high range of hypno-suggestibility. I think he has conceded to the words "moderately significantly higher" than a person without, but that is a very different thing to the classification of the high range which my friend keeps alluding to. That's not what Dr. Brown has said.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: The testimony specifically is that they are much more highly hypnotisable than the normal person. And it is upon that I must rely.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: I'm sorry, again I must object because he didn't use the word "much." Dr. Brown would not respond positively to my friend on the word "much." He said "I will accept 'moderately significantly'" more so than people without PTSD or trauma, if I understand Dr. Brown correctly. My friend is trying to exaggerate it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Blaxill, you are correct in analysing the evidence of the witness. Mr. Misetic, can we go on?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: You don't need to determine, do you, Doctor, you don't need to formally evaluate anyone in order to determine they are highly hypnotisable; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL BROWN
utterances.text: I wouldn't agree with that, no. There are standardised assessment instruments for hypnotisability, and those are generally accepted in the field. You can try to estimate it indirectly, but it is certainly not as reliable.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: In this particular case -- let's just go look at what you said on page 51 of that case.

utterances.speaker: DANIEL BROWN
utterances.text: "Case" meaning the Lauder-Grimm case?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes. You're asked a question, and the question is: "Doctor, if I can understand what you are saying there, you believe, from studies and your own experience, that a patient with a diagnosis such as the plaintiff's is likely to be highly susceptible to hypnosis, and that is including self-hypnosis." "I would say highly likely." Question: "Highly likely. But there was no study done that you have seen in this record which demonstrates that that was, in fact, the case with Ms. Lauder? You are relying on probabilities and statistical --" Your answer: "No. I am not just relying on that. Allow me to add something further to that because I think it is important to understand. There was no use of the formal laboratory or standard, formal laboratory standardised hypnotisability scales, so far as I could see in the data that I had available to me; however, we can say that we can develop some assessment of her hypnotisability based upon her response to the hypnosis, and both to Dr. Drukteinis and Dr. Grimm, she seemed to be very responsive to the hypnosis as we can gather from the notes in both of those treatments --"

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Counsel is reading too fast. The interpreters do not have any copies of these texts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: The interpreters don't have copies of these texts so they are relying on how fast you are reading and they say you are reading too fast. Can you be slower?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: "... and in that sense, we can say that without, in the absence of a formal measure of that, it is likely that she is in the high hypnotisability range. I don't see any evidence at all in the record that she was given a suggestion of hypnosis that she didn't follow." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL BROWN
utterances.text: That's correct because this is a case about dissociative identity disorder, is the main diagnosis, or multiple personality, it's not just about PTSD.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Doctor, that's not the way you qualified it in your answer and so --

utterances.speaker: DANIEL BROWN
utterances.text: I did qualify it in the answer. It also says here that she was treated with hypnosis by two different treaters and she was responsive to hypnosis all the way along through that treatment, and because hypnosis was administered, that gives us some data to assess her hypnotisability. It's not a shot in the dark. But she wasn't given a formal measure.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And right beneath that, you said -- you answered a question by saying: "That's correct, but suggestions can not only mean susceptible to suggestions by others but also to self-suggestions."

utterances.speaker: DANIEL BROWN
utterances.text: For the person with multiple personality.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Let me finish. "Both are quite possible and highly likely." Now, Dr. Brown, again you were talking in that case about the hypnotisability scale; correct?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL BROWN
utterances.text: Scales. There's a number of them, but there are standard assessment instruments, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes. And you agree that a PTSD patient is more highly hypnotisable than the average person?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL BROWN
utterances.text: Modestly so. It's the DID or the dissociative identity disorder patient who is highly hypnotisable as relevant to this particular Lauder versus Grimm case.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. But you didn't have to formally examine her. You made conclusions about reliability -- I should say "likely reliability" based on certain indicators that you obtained from the record; correct?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL BROWN
utterances.text: Indicators are history responsiveness to hypnosis but not formally assessed over a long period of treatment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Right. But you're basically saying -- you basically made an evaluation of her without examining her; correct?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL BROWN
utterances.text: In terms of a probability range, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: So what is the probability range here, Doctor?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL BROWN
utterances.text: I don't know the answer to that. I don't think there is any evidence whatsoever that she has a multiple personality, or now called dissociative identity disorder. She has some dissociative symptoms like time loss, which are common in trauma survivors, as Dr. Morgan testified about, and that I would agree with. I certainly don't think she has a major dissociative disorder as a diagnosis. And whether she has post-traumatic stress, she certainly has some post-traumatic stress symptoms. Whether she meets the full criteria, it's not fully established, but she certainly has some symptoms, and I would agree with Dr. Morgan on that. It's not established at what point in time she did have those, so that is as far as I can say from the evidence at hand.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Doctor, even in this self-induced state of hypnosis that you talked about in this case, isn't it true that it is likely, because of the suspension of critical thinking, one is much less able to distinguish between one's own internal fantasy production and actual memory of the event? Isn't it true the ability to discriminate is lost in that state?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL BROWN
utterances.text: Well, this is a compound, two questions, so I have to split it. The first part is about a self-induced state, and in the Lauder versus Grimm testimony, that's specifically referring to multiple personality disorder because there is literature documenting that self-hypnotic suggestions in causing distortion is commonly observed in patients with that diagnosis, not PTSD. The second part of the question has to do with suspension of critical thinking in hypnosis, and I would agree with that. That does happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay, Doctor. We're coming up on a break, so I'm going to ask you, during the break, if you can look through the testimony and find for us where you qualified all of these opinions on the fact that she was multiple personality and then we can talk about them after the break because, quite frankly, I can't find any qualification on your testimony in the transcripts. Isn't it true also, sir, that people who are in this higher end of the hypnotisability scale -- and we won't quibble about who is where on that scale -- actually have an increase in their confidence about the memory but a decrease in the actual accuracy of the memory?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL BROWN
utterances.text: No, that's not true. There were some studies that suggested a relationship between increased confidence and low accuracy, and now, as I've written in my book, it turns out from more recent studies that relationship is very complex and it's not as simple as that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: What is that relationship?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL BROWN
utterances.text: That high confidence and low accuracy comes in a very specific situation where there is a clear set of expectations to come up with a certain kind of response in hypnosis according to the interviewer's expectations, but in general, the relationship between confidence and accuracy is not established in the way that you suggest.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Is there a predisposition among trauma survivors for dissociation?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL BROWN
utterances.text: If I understand the question the way it's worded, dissociation is usually a personality trait, and when people are traumatised, they may draw upon their dissociative capacity as a way of dealing with the trauma.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Let me ask you a different question. If a person is asked to recount the events of what had happened to them and they're unable to recall all of the details of the event, are they likely to fill in those gaps with inaccurate recollections in addition to the real details and then believe them?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL BROWN
utterances.text: They can fill in the gaps. I don't know if likely -- I wouldn't agree with the characterisation of this as "likely" but they certainly can.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Is a person who is in this higher hypnotisability end more likely to do so?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL BROWN
utterances.text: Only in certain situations. It's not as simple as that. If they are in a context where the interviewer expects them to fill in the gaps, then, of course, they will. For example, in Dr. Morgan's more recent study of the Gulf War, when it was clear that he expected his respondents to give an answer for their inconsistencies; in that context of being expected to come up with an answer, they're going to come up with an answer, not necessarily the right answer. But in general, that doesn't occur.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: For example, if you are being questioned by a war crimes investigator to recall specific details of things, that would be one such type situation where you are being asked to recall the details; correct?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL BROWN
utterances.text: That could be a situation, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: So a person who is in this state is more likely to have manufactured facts --

utterances.speaker: DANIEL BROWN
utterances.text: His state, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: State of hypnotisability or hypnosis, better. A person in the state of hypnosis and questioned about specific details and specific events by a war crimes investigator is more likely to manufacture the details to the extent that she can't recall them?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL BROWN
utterances.text: Again, the problem is with "more likely." It would depend upon the context of expectations that the war crimes investigator had. That's certainly the case. But if they were expected to come up with answers for which they were -- about events for which they were quite uncertain, that that could be a situation where you're going to get memory distortion. I would agree with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Could one such line of questioning include the specific names of individuals, the places where criminal acts occurred, the timing of those criminal acts; isn't that possible?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL BROWN
utterances.text: It's possible, but when you get to details like names and places, it's more likely to happen when the interviewer is supplying that as misinformation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Right. So, for example, let's speak hypothetically in this case.

utterances.speaker: DANIEL BROWN
utterances.text: It's possible, but the question really here is: How possible? In terms of misinformation suggestion effects in the general population, the range runs around 3 to 5 per cent of individuals. If we talk about it in terms of a diagnosis of post-traumatic stress, the Levitt study that I testified about this morning suggests that abused individuals may be significantly less suggestible. Of course, it's possible, but it's a low range of possibility here.

utterances.speaker: DANIEL BROWN
utterances.text: I think it's low possibility --

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: I must object to that question, Your Honours. This appears to be crossing the line to the point that he is actually suggesting what had happened in those circumstances. I mean, he can put a question as to "What do you think the effect of a war crimes investigator" or something like that, but I think it's going too far to suggest that he's helping her along with the details in that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: It's hypothetical.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic, we have considered this line of cross-examination. There is, of course, no evidence to support the suggestions which you are making, which, in any event, are common-sense matters. If you are suggesting a witness might have been influenced by the questions put by an investigator, well, of course, that could be the case. As I have said, there is no evidence to support any such suggestion, but if you wish to put those submissions to us by way of comment, of course, we will consider them. But they are matters for submission. They are not, in my judgement, matters for expert evidence, and I have to say that I do not find this cross-examination helpful, of assistance to us in trying the case. Now, as I say, if you want to make the comments, you can, but I think it's time that we moved on to some other area. We have spent a very long time on this other case, this New Hampshire case, and if you have some other areas to explore, it would be helpful to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Dr. Brown, there was reference made this morning to your book, "Memory, Trauma, Treatment and the Law"; correct?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL BROWN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And one of the questions was how well-received this book had been in the United States, correct, or generally?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL BROWN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Doctor, one of your co-authors on this book is Dr. Corydon Hammond; correct?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL BROWN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And Dr. Corydon Hammond is a firm believer in the recovered memory phenomenon; correct?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL BROWN
utterances.text: You have to clarify what you mean by the stereotype "recovered memory phenomena."

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: That it is possible to have a traumatic event, completely forget about that traumatic event, and then remember that traumatic event at some point in the future.

utterances.speaker: DANIEL BROWN
utterances.text: I can't really talk about Dr. Hammond's beliefs in any detail, but what you're describing, forgetting trauma and then completely forgetting it and then later recovering the memory for it, it's well-documented in the field, and I assume that Dr. Hammond believes that and I certainly agree with that because that's what the evidence shows.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And as part of this debate, it's true, is it not, that it's necessary to establish that memories are indelible in some way, that they can't be forgotten; isn't that the essential gist of the argument?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL BROWN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: What is the gist of the argument?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL BROWN
utterances.text: Indelibility usually refers to what's called the emotional -- or implicit emotional or behavioural memory, not to the narrative memory for the trauma. There's two different types of traumatic memory here.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: So which one are you saying is one that is always constant or present?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL BROWN
utterances.text: The emotional or behavioural implicit memory is the one that's usually referred to as indelible.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, it's true, is it not, that your co-author, Dr. Hammond, has been named a co-conspirator of a $65 million fraud case by the United States government; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL BROWN
utterances.text: I don't know that to be true.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic, what has that got to do with this case?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I'm trying to get at how credible the book is and what the underlying motives for establishing --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: That's a criminal case you're talking about. It has nothing to do with the scientific research this expert has discussed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Can we have a break just so I can get to the hippocampus material, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. We shall have a break for 20 minutes, in which case we shall come back at 16.05.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're going to need to collect, unfortunately, the copies of D39 which were passed out so that we can put them back together again.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Before cross-examination continues, we had indicated that we might possibly recall Witness A. We want to inform the Court that we are releasing Witness A, and we do not intend to recall her. We would ask the Court's permission that she be allowed to return home.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. She can return back home. Yes, Mr. Misetic, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes. These are the copies of the relevant portions of the transcript.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for Mr. Misetic, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Your microphone, Mr. Misetic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry. This is just with that area I'll follow-up on, the hippocampus, and then I'll move on.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This will be marked D39.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Sir, I'm referring to page 87, and rather than read that preceding question, I'll try to say where you were in terms of your thoughts at that time. If you disagree, you can stop, and I'll read the whole thing in. You were talking, I believe, at the top of the page about PET scanning, which, I believe, is a type of brain scan.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic, D39 is referred to as draft testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes, but it's certified, Your Honour. If he disagrees that it was his testimony, I'll take that into account.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: The question is: "It's like -- is a PET scan like kind of an extra type photo -- Answer: Yes, except it's a live action shot. When the person is performing some sort of task, you can actually look at what areas of the brain light up and you can see what areas of the brain are being enlisted for that given task, specifically -- under the presumption that blood flow -- the more blood flow to the area which you're showing radioactively means that the area of the brain is being more active. Under that presumption then, we can look at what areas of the brain become active for a given task, and there are two areas of the brain that are associated with memory. One is associated with memory for factual information, narrative memory, hippocampus," misspelled, "and then there is the part of the brain that essentially processes emotional memory. That's called the amygdala. Essentially, what this study showed was that during flashbacks, irrespective of the type of trauma, as compared to when the person was not flashing back, using the subject as their own control, that during the flashbacks, these eight individuals were showing virtually no left brain verbal activity and were showing activity primarily in the two areas of the brain. One was the amygdala or emotional memory processing system, and the other were the sensory cortex areas of the brain, and they were showing virtually no left brain activity and no hippocampal activity. Question: So what are we saying? Answer: The implication it seems to be a neuro-biological -- piece of neuro-biological evidence that justifies the fact that traumatic memories are processed by the brain differently than normal memories, simply by virtue of their emotional process, so they are processed more in the emotional and sensory centres of the brain and they are processed less in the verbal portion of the brain." Then it goes on, "That seems to be consistent with our patients and our view of survivors' reports of having flashbacks and sensory experiences when they first recover memories and having an incomplete or no narrative memory. Because what the PET scan study shows is something quite consistent with those clinical reports." Now, Dr. Brown, I realise that that text does not state that you think there is a shrinkage in the hippocampus; however, is it not true then that there is a problem with the hippocampus in terms of a person who has been traumatised?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL BROWN
utterances.text: I wouldn't characterise it that way. There are two types of studies. There are the structural studies which show, actually, damage to the hippocampus in terms of the hippocampal volume. Those were the kind of studies that Dr. Morgan was testifying about and which I really question the evidence. The second type of studies are what are called functional or process studies where you can actually look at areas of the brain that are active during a given task. This testimony in the Quattrocchi case refers very specifically to a functional, not a structural, study, and all it simply suggests is that during a flashback episode, the processing is largely in the sensory and emotional areas of the brain, consistent with a patient's report that they get a more emotional and more sensory experience of the flashback with less of a narrative report. That doesn't tell us anything about the rest of the time when they are not flashing back, what their brain activity is like relative to the hippocampus and their narrative memory. This is specific to when people have flashbacks, and it certainly doesn't imply anything about brain damage to the hippocampus.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: You use the term "brain damage." Is it not correct, though, that, from your perspective, brain activity in a traumatised patient is different than brain activity in a normal patient, in a healthy patient?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL BROWN
utterances.text: Brain activity during flashbacks, I would certainly agree with that. That was my testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Dr. Brown, how many papers have you published on Post Traumatic Stress Disorder?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL BROWN
utterances.text: Mostly books, not papers, or chapters of books.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: In writing a chapter of a book, you're basically recounting the work of others in the field; correct?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL BROWN
utterances.text: Most of my writing has been textbooks, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: How much research have you done in the area of Post Traumatic Stress Disorder?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL BROWN
utterances.text: Most of my work has been as a clinician and as a teacher. That's my appointment at Harvard Medical School. I'm not engaged actively in very much research, mostly teaching and clinical responsibilities.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: You said "not very much research." How much research have you actually done in your entire career?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL BROWN
utterances.text: At the start of my career, I had a post-graduate grant from the National Institute of Mental Health, where I did -- a two-year grant. I did some clinical research. Shortly after finishing that, I took the post as director of training and eventually as chief psychologist at the Cambridge Hospital, one of the Harvard teaching hospitals. That particular track was clinical responsibilities, running a major internship centre for psychologists, and mostly teaching. So I haven't done that much active research since.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Have you written any papers of any kind in terms of primary research within the last eight years?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL BROWN
utterances.text: In terms of experimentally designed studies, I don't think so, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: What is your experience in the area of Post Traumatic Stress Disorder?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL BROWN
utterances.text: I've treated patients with Post Traumatic Stress Disorder for well over 20 years, starting extensively going back to about 1978, with a woman by the name of Sarah Hailey who was a consultant I first learned trauma from. She was one of the originators of the diagnosis of PTSD for DSM. Since the late 70s, I've had an active practice involving treating trauma patients. My practice is about -- since then, it's been about 25 patients a week, and about 60 to 70 per cent of those have been trauma patients of one sort or another, a cross --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: But not specifically PTSD?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL BROWN
utterances.text: Oh, no, over half of my patients have been either with major diagnoses of PTSD or a major dissociative disorder.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could we ask the witness to slow down, please?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL BROWN
utterances.text: That is, the trauma-related diagnoses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, you are reminded to slow down by the interpreter.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: What is meant by the term "peer review"?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL BROWN
utterances.text: "Peer review" generally means that you author papers and you submit those papers to journals which have an independently set of refereed individuals who will evaluate the paper.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If a paper has been peer reviewed, that would mean then that independent individuals have reviewed the paper for its legitimacy?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL BROWN
utterances.text: It means that they reviewed it, gave comments on it, and accepted it for publication, either with or without modifications.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, I'm going to ask you about some studies with respect to the hippocampal shrinkage, and I'd ask for your opinion on each of them. The Bremner study in 1995, are you familiar with that study?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL BROWN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And your position on that is?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL BROWN
utterances.text: I think I gave testimony about that this morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Which is?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL BROWN
utterances.text: Briefly, I think there is some problem with the measurement using a mouse cursor technique and not reporting what the error rate is when the magnitude of the effect is so small. Subsequently, it turns out that there was some miscalculation in the statistics, and the results didn't reach statistical significance, and there was a retraction letter by Bremner in, I think, June of 1997 in the American Journal of Psychiatry about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Isn't it true, though, that subsequent to that he republished the study to take into account the error?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL BROWN
utterances.text: My recollection is that the significance level with the recalculation was .06, which does not meet the criteria for statistical significance.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Is that your recollection or is that what the study says?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL BROWN
utterances.text: That's my recollection.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: That was a study of women with PTSD; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL BROWN
utterances.text: This particular study, the '95?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: The '97, the republished version?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL BROWN
utterances.text: I don't think I've seen the republished version.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: You just said that --

utterances.speaker: DANIEL BROWN
utterances.text: I've seen the study and I've seen the retraction letter. That's all I've seen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Right. But then I asked you about the subsequent study, which is the Bremner '97, that took into account the error that was in Bremner '95, and you said that it still had a .06 error rate?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL BROWN
utterances.text: Yes, but I haven't seen the study.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: How do you know that it has a. 06 error rate?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL BROWN
utterances.text: In discussion with one of my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Are you familiar with the Gurewitz study of 1997 which measured hippocampal shrinkage in PTSD patients?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL BROWN
utterances.text: Yes, but I don't remember it very well. It was originally presented at the International Society of Traumatic Stress, and that's the version I heard of. I haven't seen a written version of this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: That was published and peer reviewed?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL BROWN
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Cambie (phoen) 1997, I'd ask for your comment on that, the reported shrinkage in the hippocampus of individuals with PTSD?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL BROWN
utterances.text: Again, my familiarity with these studies was at a symposium at the International Society of Traumatic Stress. I haven't seen the publication of some of these studies since.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Do you know whether they were published or peer reviewed?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL BROWN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: There was a study of women with PTSD and shrinkage of the hippocampus by Stein in 1997. Have you reviewed that document?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL BROWN
utterances.text: I haven't reviewed the document, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Are you familiar with the study?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL BROWN
utterances.text: I think that was a study of long-term effects of childhood sexual abuse, and there was evidence of hippocampal damage, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Was that published and peer reviewed?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL BROWN
utterances.text: I don't remember the source of it. Again, most of these I've gotten through the International Society of Traumatic Stress symposium when they were presented publicly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Has anyone told you then, if you haven't seen the studies, that both the Stein 1997 and Bremner 1997 studies were with women with no history of alcohol abuse?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL BROWN
utterances.text: I think they are still long-term studies. I didn't testify that all of these were alcohol related, but there were studies of effects over long periods of time, as opposed to the MacFarlane study, which is in the time frame in question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Are you familiar with Science Magazine?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL BROWN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: What is your opinion of its reputation in the field?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL BROWN
utterances.text: It's one of the tops.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic, we are wondering to what extent all of your questions are relevant to our case, because there's been no allegations so far that Witness A has got any shrinkage in her hippocampus. There was no medical examination. We really wonder whether it is relevant to ask so many questions to this witness or to dwell on this matter generally.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: You heard the expert testimony of Dr. Morgan. It was put in a dispute as to this issue. The fact that there is no examination of Witness A, I would agree that that is a handicap, but in light of that fact, I'm left to discuss what PTSD is, what the effects of PTSD are, its symptoms, and its physical results. To the extent that the witness has put it in issue, I would like to just put it to him to see whether he has referred to these studies, and then the Court can take it into consideration as it wishes. I will move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: But this is speculative, hypothetical, and academic. Could you move on, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Dr. Brown, one of your criticisms, I believe, of Dr. Morgan was that there was no baseline. If you didn't testify to that, I believe it's in your statement; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL BROWN
utterances.text: I think what you're referring to, and let's clarify it together here, that in the Desert Storm study, there was no military record by which to compare the one-month, two-month, or the two-year reports against, to check for accuracy. So this is not a study of accuracy. It's specifically about inconsistency. Is that what you're referring to by "baseline"?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes. What I'm wondering is why we need to find the medical files of an individual to determine what really happened if we can rely on the memories of the individuals who answered the study?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL BROWN
utterances.text: Well, I think I testified that in all cases of memory, we can't say that they correspond to historically accurate events without corroboration. In this case, in order to do research specifically on the issue of accuracy, there has to be some documented objective event. However well documented or not, we can have different standards of evidence, but there has to be some baseline of documentation by which to compare this against, and without that, the research can't legitimately make any statements about accuracy.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Doctor. I'd ask you not to refer to any of the charts that you reviewed or anything that's within the charts themselves, but you talked about sequencing errors?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL BROWN
utterances.text: By "charts," do you mean Dr. Morgan's charts, Exhibits 32A through D or E?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: DANIEL BROWN
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Aren't sequencing errors an important aspect of the accuracy of memory?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL BROWN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Explain that.

utterances.speaker: DANIEL BROWN
utterances.text: Well, let's say we have four items. In order to check accuracy, we would have to compare those items to some historical event. Let's say, in a laboratory, we had subjects view a film of a burglary, and there were four things that they could have observed. Accuracy would mean that when they gave the report, the four things that they reported were corresponding to the original stimulus event in the film, but they might get the order of those four events mixed up. So the misordering doesn't imply inaccuracy.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Please slow down. Please slow down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Slow down again.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: You're aware, are you not, of the identification that Witness A made of Mr. Furundzija in 1995?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL BROWN
utterances.text: What document are you referring to specifically?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: The witness statement of Witness A from July of 1995? That's not it.

utterances.speaker: DANIEL BROWN
utterances.text: I know. I just have my own notes to tag what they refer to. This is the July 1995 witness statement we're referring to; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: DANIEL BROWN
utterances.text: Yesyes,.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. I'll side-track here, since you've cited that study again. I'm reading here from John Yuille 1986. The copyright is 1986. I'm not sure what the year is on it. Correct? Do you have a copy of that?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL BROWN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: My copy does not have any page number -- yes, it does. 296. It's in the upper left-hand corner.

utterances.speaker: DANIEL BROWN
utterances.text: I'm sorry, what page again?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Two nine six.

utterances.speaker: DANIEL BROWN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: First, would you agree with me that this study is not about PTSD?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL BROWN
utterances.text: No, I wouldn't agree. It's about a stressful event that had a major impact on the eyewitness's life, and it may or may not have involved PTSD. It just wasn't measured.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: So therefore it's not a study of PTSD patients per se.

utterances.speaker: DANIEL BROWN
utterances.text: No, that wasn't part of the study. That doesn't imply that with events of that magnitude that some of the eyewitnesses wouldn't have PTSD.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, I call your attention to the second column on that page, the first full paragraph: "Just under 40 per cent of the details provided the researchers were also given to the police. Of this total, 81.56 per cent were consistent in the two interviews." So isn't it more accurate to say that people forgot 60 per cent, remembered 40 per cent, and then you were measuring the consistency -- not you, I'm sorry, Yuille -- was measuring the consistency of the 40 per cent of the information that was reported initially?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL BROWN
utterances.text: No, that's not accurate at all. The baseline data which was the composite constructed by the police was the baseline of which the later memory was compared and there was a 60 per cent increase in new information reported at the five- to six-months mark, so that they're saying 40 per cent here because that's comparing it the other way, but basically there was an increase in the information the other time, a 60 per cent increase over time that was accurate for the most part.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Let me get back to what our original question was, which was with respect to the identification. Now, you agree that that is a difference; correct?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL BROWN
utterances.text: Please clarify "that."

utterances.speaker: DANIEL BROWN
utterances.text: Fair enough.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, how do we know which person Witness A saw?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: That's not for this witness to answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I'm asking for his expertise in how to distinguish between the two. Which one is the one that is more correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: No, no, no. This witness can't answer that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: From a purely scientific perspective, not -- I'm trying to arrive at the methodology of how he would make the evaluation, not whether it's right or wrong.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: That is not for this type of witness, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: What types of things can take into -- might change a person's identification over a three-year period?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL BROWN
utterances.text: My testimony has been and still is that identification of things like hair colour, height, weight, colour of clothing, and the massive body of scientific literature we have about that isn't very good in the first place, and the Court needs to be aware that these are commonly observed memory mistakes in the research. It's for the triers of fact, of course, to determine from there the more onerous task of whether these identifications of Witness A are accurate or not, but they are, in the literature, shown to be imperfect around such details as height and hair colour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I understand that, Doctor. But what I'm asking you is, what can change a person's recollection? Is there a basis upon which a person would change an identification from one set of characteristics to another?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL BROWN
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Now I understand your question. My answer would be that the memory for such details is sometimes uncertain in the first place, so it would change as a function of the uncertainty of the memory.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Are there any prompts or things like that, suggestible influences or something that could change a person's ID, perhaps even coming into the courtroom or -- forget the courtroom setting, perhaps seeing the person?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL BROWN
utterances.text: It's again possible, but these things change anyway because the memories for such details isn't very certain in the first place for some individuals.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I'd like to call your attention again to one study that you mentioned in your direct examination and that's, I believe, Groeneweg study, which is the study of the Nazi concentration camp survivors?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL BROWN
utterances.text: It's Wagenaar and Groeneweg, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, when you talk about consistency of memory for gist, you're talking about the fact that a person generally remembers they were in a camp, they were tortured, that they had a certain routine every day that they had to do of some sort; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL BROWN
utterances.text: Well, the torture might fall under the category of injury specific amnesia which was reported in that study, but consistency in that particular study had to do with the kind of things you're talking about, which was the severity of the exposure to cold, the starvation, the difficult work routines, yes, and the general sense of mistreatment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: But with respect to specific details about names of people, about physical characteristics, and even photo recognition of the actual war criminal who was committing the torture, those memories had changed; correct?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL BROWN
utterances.text: For such details, that's correct, after 40 years.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Things like physical characteristics, names, photo recognition of a person are all outside of gist and are part of the peripheral detail; correct?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL BROWN
utterances.text: Not necessarily. My testimony was that gist in the research literature is defined in terms of central actions, plot relevance, and personal meaningfulness, so if a particular action happened that involved a given individual that had a great deal of impact on the person's life or was relevant to the plot of what happened in some other way, it might be clearly defined as gist. It depends on the situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: But wouldn't you characterise things like photo identification, names of the camp guards, and details of the individual's physical make-up to be unique idiosyncratic details?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL BROWN
utterances.text: In general, that's correct, but, for example, in the case here, it may be the case that, as Witness A testified to being sadistically raped and tortured, that the interview that was the cause of that rape occurring would be plot relevant and therefore the details made be encoded differently with a stronger memory. So, you see, it depends on things like plot relevance and meaningfulness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: But that wouldn't be the case for the Nazi war criminal in the Groeneweg study?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL BROWN
utterances.text: After 40 years, it's hard to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Were you present in the courtroom on Monday, sir?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL BROWN
utterances.text: No, I was not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Have you had any update as to Witness A's testimony in this case on Monday?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL BROWN
utterances.text: I haven't had a chance to look at that transcript, so I'd have to say no.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: With respect to -- I know you haven't seen the transcript, but has anyone told you generally what had happened?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL BROWN
utterances.text: I couldn't comment on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: May I interpose for just one second? I hesitate to interrupt my friend in full flow, but are we going to be close to issues that may require private or closed session? I just pose that as an interrogatory at this stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Closed session is fine with me -- I mean private session. We can just turn the sound off. I'm not using any boards or any physical evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: I'm asking you, are you going to go into the details of the evidence that was in closed session?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Generally, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: We'll go into a private session.

utterances.speaker: DANIEL BROWN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: You were asked, indeed you were pressed by Defence counsel in the level of hypnotisability you would attribute or you attributed to the person in that evidence?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL BROWN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Sir, could you read a portion that starts, I think, at line 13.

utterances.speaker: DANIEL BROWN
utterances.text: On page 49?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes, sir. This would be page 49 at this point.

utterances.speaker: DANIEL BROWN
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Do you, in fact, make reference below there, at line 18 and 19, to the 12-point scale of hypnotisability?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL BROWN
utterances.text: Yes. That refers to the Stanford Hypnotic Susceptibility Scale, Form C.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: What in that testimony did you say in relation to the figure that is applicable to Post Traumatic Stress Disorder persons?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL BROWN
utterances.text: I said that the usual responses were a score about -- in the testimony it says "would be 8 or 9"; exactly it's 8.5 is the mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: In fact, if I look up to line 19 and 20 on page 49, you make reference to another number, do you not, in respect of normal people?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL BROWN
utterances.text: That's 5.5 for normal individuals, usually.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And you said that was consistent with what you said in your evidence in chief earlier on?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL BROWN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Sir, moving on, on page 50 of that document, you refer to people of multiple personality disorder, do you not?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL BROWN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And people of that disorder, you classify, do you not, at lines 4 and 5 in the regions of being 10 out of the 12-point scale?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL BROWN
utterances.text: It's actually 10.5, but, yes, between 10 and 12. They're in the very high range of hypnotisability generally.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Fine. You then -- considering, therefore, the level of hypnotisability of such people, can you tell us just a little bit more about that? What is the diagnosis of MPD?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL BROWN
utterances.text: The diagnosis of MPD, as was given in the Diagnostic Statistics Manual, version III, and the revised version of III, its name got changed to Dissociative Identity Disorder in the fourth version which came out in 1994, so there are slight differences in the diagnostic criteria, but it usually means the presence of two or more altered personality states which take executive control of the person, has a significant shift in their state of consciousness, and altered personalities come out and take executive control for some degree of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: We all know that you had no opportunity of a clinical assessment of Witness A in this case, but from the materials you have reviewed and all you have listened to in connection with this case, can you make any comment in respect of the question of MPD, multiple personality disorder? Has it any relevance?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL BROWN
utterances.text: I could find no evidence whatsoever that Witness A showed any signs of a major dissociative disorder like multiple personality disorder.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Fine. Thank you. Could we move on to page 52, 53, and did you, in fact, make reference in that testimony to the specific hypnotisability of the female party to that litigation?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL BROWN
utterances.text: Yes. It says at the bottom of 52, line 21 and 22: "It is likely that she is in the high hypnotisability range." And that's based on the -- the likely diagnosis of multiple personality in this particular individual.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: When we get to -- if you would turn to page 115, sir?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL BROWN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: You made a reference regarding hypnosis and responses in hypnosis, and on page 116, did you make any reference to the pattern of suggestibility you say was relevant in this particular case? If so, would you read the relevant few lines?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL BROWN
utterances.text: Well, actually, it starts on 114. It starts at line 21 on 114.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: So the whole passage, you say, is relevant to that issue?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL BROWN
utterances.text: Yes. "... we have a number of entries in Michaela Williams' notes," that's the massage therapist," ... a number of entries ... that the dissatisfaction was sexual, but that information is supplied in every example in the journal by Michaela Williams and not by Ms. Lauder. That's an example of leading suggestions." That is, more than one. There's a pattern.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: You then talked about some relevant research, sir. Could you read out your -- appears a conclusion in your evidence, or at least a summary, a summation, around line -- from the end of line 5 down to line 8?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL BROWN
utterances.text: On page ...

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: On page 116 now, sir.

utterances.speaker: DANIEL BROWN
utterances.text: Okay. The conclusion really starts on line 2: "And where we get a combination of vulnerability for pseudo-memory or the confabulation," that is, the high hypnotisability in this multiple personality patient, "that is the decreased ability to discriminate fantasy and memory accuracy." In such a patient --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Slowly, please. Slow down, please?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL BROWN
utterances.text: "... that, you get a clear evidence of --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Slow down for the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: DANIEL BROWN
utterances.text: "... you get a clear evidence of a history of leading suggestions which goes over a number of months of those notes," referring back to the massage therapist.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Dr. Brown, if we could turn to the second volume of that document, and on page 276, I think it is.

utterances.speaker: DANIEL BROWN
utterances.text: Two hundred and seventy-six?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes, sir. Two seven six, yes. Sir, you make certain references regarding self-hypnosis.

utterances.speaker: DANIEL BROWN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And dissociation and going into a trance-like state.

utterances.speaker: DANIEL BROWN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Could you just confirm whether you were giving that evidence in relation to the actual activities of the person in question?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL BROWN
utterances.text: Well, yes, and this refers specifically again to the diagnosis of multiple personality disorder, and I probably should enter into the record, because Defence counsel asked me to find the pages for the multiple personality disorder, that's on page 26, starting on line 3: "He then referred Ms. Lauder to Dr. Grimm and Dr. Grimm appropriately carried forth the same diagnosis of chronic Post Traumatic Stress Disorder. Now, in the course of treatment, what seemed to emerge were different alters and he recently considered a diagnosis of multiple personality disorder, in addition to the diagnosis of Post Traumatic Stress Disorder." There are numerous other references of the treatment of that patient involving treatment around multiple personality but that suffices, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: But then just to encapsulate the evidence you gave in that particular case, on pages 276 and 277, you do cover the topics, it seems, of going into trance-like states when --

utterances.speaker: DANIEL BROWN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And that if something upsetting comes up, she could go into altered states?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL BROWN
utterances.text: Shifting states is a common diagnostic feature of multiple personality disorder.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And then moving on on 277 to the issue of confabulation with a personality of that type. Is that so, sir?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL BROWN
utterances.text: Confabulation and self-suggested distortions in their memory is well-documented in that population.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On page 279, Doctor, if I have it correctly, I sincerely hope my reference is correct, did you make reference in that evidence to the actual use of self-hypnosis by this lady? I may have the wrong page but ...

utterances.speaker: DANIEL BROWN
utterances.text: I don't seem to find it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I thought it was 279, but nor can I now. Is that, in fact, relevant to a certain issue? Did this lady, rather, practice actual self-hypnosis?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL BROWN
utterances.text: Yes, I think she did, and as a result of doing that over a long period of time, along with the pattern of misinformation supplied to her, it caused significant distortion in her memory.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: So indeed, in fact, that is another reference on page 276, I see it's at line 4. I thank you for that, Doctor. There's just one final thing which is a comment in relation to the testimony you gave in the other case by name of Quattrocchi, I think it is.

utterances.speaker: DANIEL BROWN
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And the reference to page 88 in that transcript, just to confirm it is correct, Doctor, you say that the PET scan research appears to have involved -- only a maximum of eight people carried out that test; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL BROWN
utterances.text: No, the research included eight subjects of different types of trauma from combat trauma to childhood sexual abuse to rape.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: There were eight subjects?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL BROWN
utterances.text: Yeah, PET scanning research is extremely expensive so usually it has small numbers of subjects.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Thank you. I have nothing further. I'm obliged, Your Honours. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, in light of the fact that now both parties have relied on these two transcripts, we would offer them in.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be D39 and D40. I don't know if the Prosecutor wants to have his exhibits admitted as well, Exhibit 12 and 13?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: We remain with one more witness in rebuttal for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Ma'am, the position at this time is that I do know, if we can confirm we are fully cleared with Dr. Brown, I know he has urgent business in Washington, D.C., and a release from this Court would be much desired at this time as he has to fly out tomorrow morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Anything from the Defence? Any objection to releasing Dr. Brown?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Dr. Brown. You are free to go.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: That concludes my part at this time. My learned colleague Ms. Patricia Sellers is going to be leading the next witness for the Prosecution, Ma'am.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, the Trial Chamber actually intends to adjourn because we started very early today at 9.00 with other cases, so we will resume this proceedings tomorrow at 0930 hours. But I wish to inform the parties that immediately after completing the testimony in this case, we expect the parties to make their closing remarks.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Noted, Ma'am.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: So the Court will adjourn until tomorrow, 0930 hours.

utterances.speaker: THE USHER
utterances.text: All rise.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: We apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, you can go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: We intended to call at least one witness back in rejoinder --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, after the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Just to be clear. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: 5.10 p.m., to be reconvened on Thursday, the 12th day of November, 1998, at 9.30 a.m.
